subject: History
description: Covers Lost-wax casting and Steatite seals.

questions.stem: The famous dancing girl statuette found at Mohenjo-Daro, a masterpiece of the Indus Valley Civilization, was made using which highly advanced metallurgical technique?
questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The 4,500-year-old bronze 'Dancing Girl' was created using the 'Lost-Wax' (cire-perdue) casting technique. In this intricate method, a wax model is covered with clay, baked to melt and drain out the wax (hence 'lost-wax'), and then molten bronze is poured into the resulting hollow clay mold. This proves the Harappans possessed incredibly sophisticated metallurgical science.
DECOY BUSTING: The Harappans did NOT know about Iron (the Iron Age in India started much later during the Vedic period). While they made terracotta toys, the Dancing Girl is explicitly bronze.
EXAM INSIGHT: The same lost-wax technique was perfected thousands of years later by the Chola Dynasty in South India to create their world-renowned Nataraja (dancing Shiva) bronze sculptures.

questions.stem: Most of the square seals discovered at various Harappan sites, which feature intricate animal motifs and undeciphered script, were primarily carved out of which material?
questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The vast majority of the thousands of Harappan seals discovered were made of Steatite, a soft metamorphic rock commonly known as soapstone. Because it is incredibly soft and easy to carve, but hardens significantly when baked, it was the perfect medium for creating highly detailed intaglio seals (like the famous 'Pashupati' seal).
DECOY BUSTING: Lapis Lazuli was a highly prized blue stone imported from Afghanistan for jewelry, but rarely used for standard seals. Terracotta was used for pottery and toys, but lacked the precision needed for official seals.
EXAM INSIGHT: These seals were primarily used for commercial purposes (stamping clay tags on trade goods) and as amulets. The script on them remains one of the great undeciphered mysteries of ancient history.
